_meta.description: The cohort clock — the master time axis for the whole dashboard. Age-band populations projected forward, the spending shape within each band, and which limbs each band pays. Every other panel is indexed to this.
_meta.source_note: Population figures are Census-projection-shaped estimates entered from memory and MUST be replaced with the current Census vintage before publication as fact. The SHAPE of the curve — 75-84 growing hardest through 2035, 85+ nearly doubling by 2040, 65-74 flat-to-down after 2030 — is robust to vintage and is what the thesis rests on.

now.headline: Median boomer is 71. The cohort's centre of mass is crossing out of go-go and into slow-go.
now.body: This is the single most important sentence on the dashboard. The leading edge of the cohort turned 80 this year; the trailing edge is 62 and still working. The median sits at 71 — right at the boundary where discretionary travel and leisure spending rolls over and healthcare, home services and care spending begins its climb. The experience-economy trade has had its demographic tailwind. The care trade still has one.

cohort_edges.note: Now entering the band where mortality and care transitions begin to cluster. First-step wealth transfers — to surviving spouses — are happening at scale.
The largest single cohort in the wave. Sits at the top of the go-go band today; crosses into slow-go around 2032.
The centre of mass. Its position is the clock hand for the entire limb-D relay.
Still working, still accumulating, still contributing to plans. This is why limb A's flow reversal is gradual rather than a step.
Turns 65 in 2030. The pipeline behind the cohort — the reason the thesis outlives the boomer label.

bands.label: Peak earning, peak accumulating
bands.behaviour: Highest household income and highest contribution rates. Catch-up contributions, mortgage payoff, last major durable purchases. Still net suppliers of capital to markets and net suppliers of labour.
bands.note: Gen X occupies this band for the whole thesis horizon. It is what stops limb A from being a cliff.

bands.label: Peak discretionary — time-rich, health-intact, asset-rich
bands.behaviour: Travel, cruises, RVs and boats, second homes, golf and leisure, restaurants, elective and quality-of-life procedures (joints, cataracts, dental, hearing). Spending total is only slightly below working life but the mix is radically different. Housing decisions begin — downsizing, relocation to retirement metros.
bands.note: The cohort's centre of mass has been sitting here. It is leaving. Fade into strength rather than shorting — earnings roll over after the demography does.

bands.label: Total spend falls, mix rotates hard into care
bands.behaviour: Travel and discretionary durables drop away. Healthcare share of the basket climbs steeply — chronic disease management, cardiology, ophthalmology, sensory aids, mobility. Home services and home modification replace DIY. First care decisions: in-home help, then possibly a move. Driving stops. This is the band with the steepest population growth through 2035.
bands.note: The fastest-growing band on the clock, and the one the cohort is entering now. This is where the thesis's demographic wind is strongest.

bands.label: Medical and long-term care dominate; asset release becomes forced
bands.behaviour: Spending concentrates almost entirely in medical, long-term care and housing-with-care. Care intensity rises sharply and so does its labour content. Assets are released not by choice but by care costs or by death — this is where the transfer in limb B actually executes, and where the housing stock in limb H is finally released.
bands.note: Nearly doubles by 2040. The most labour-intensive band to serve, which is where limb C and limb D collide directly.

reading.body: Slow-go (75–84) grows by roughly a third between 2025 and 2035, and 85+ roughly doubles between 2025 and 2040. Meanwhile go-go (65–74) peaks around 2030 and then declines. The demographic wind is not 'aging' in general — it is specifically behind the two oldest bands and specifically against the youngest retired one.

Businesses serving 65–74 are trading against a tailwind that expires around 2030. Businesses serving 75+ have a tailwind that runs past 2040. Same 'aging' narrative, opposite gradient, and the market prices them as one theme.

Care hours consumed scale with the 85+ band, not with the 65+ total. A near-doubling of 85+ against a care workforce whose training pipeline is capacity-constrained is the arithmetic behind limb C — and the margin problem inside limb D.

relay.n: The go-go band is still large but has stopped growing
relay.beneficiaries: Cruise, travel, RV/marine, active-adult housing, elective ortho and ophthalmic, golf and leisure
relay.stance: Harvest. Fade into strength. The population supporting these businesses peaks and then turns.

relay.n: The slow-go band takes the growth baton
relay.beneficiaries: Home health, chronic care management, sensory (hearing/vision), cardiology and structural heart, mobility, home modification, LTC pharmacy, Medicare Advantage
relay.stance: Accumulate. This is the core of the book and the demographic wind is strongest here.

relay.beneficiaries: Skilled nursing, memory care, hospice, senior housing with care, death care, estate and trust services, the transfer itself
relay.stance: Build early where valuation allows — the demand is arithmetic, the constraint is labour and reimbursement, so own the ones that survive both.

wealth_split.note: The cohort is not one customer. Concentration within it means the top decile and the median retiree face opposite problems, and a single 'the retiree' framing produces wrong positions for one of them. Universe records are tagged with which customer they serve.

segments.share_note: Holds the large majority of cohort net worth
segments.problem: Estate and tax efficiency, not income adequacy. Will not decumulate meaningfully — dies holding.
segments.serves: Trust and estate services, private banking, alternatives access, luxury and legacy spending, philanthropy infrastructure

segments.share_note: Materially under-saved relative to a full-length retirement
segments.problem: Income adequacy and out-of-pocket care cost. Will decumulate, will rely on Social Security and Medicare, and is directly exposed to limb E policy risk.
segments.serves: Annuities and guaranteed income, Medicare Advantage, value retail and dollar stores, generic pharmacy, reverse mortgage, subsidised and middle-market senior housing
